Canada training credit: how the CAD 250 a year builds up, how much of a course comes back, and whether waiting pays

Use CRA’s Canada training credit rules to see how your limit grows, why the credit refunds half of course fees up to that limit, how it reduces your tuition amount, and what delaying a course really adds.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 8 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Plan a Canada training credit claim: how much of your course fees come back, and whether waiting adds more

Interactive planning lab

Canada training credit for the whole course (refundable)$2,000
Federal tuition tax credit on the remaining fees, at 14%$560
Total federal relief on the fees$2,560
Federal relief without the training credit$840
Fees left after federal relief$3,440
Training credit limit left for 2028$250

Fees of $6,000 over 2 study years from 2026 earn $2,000 of Canada training credit, paid even if you owe no tax, and a 14% federal tuition credit of $560 on the $4,000 left. Without the training credit the tuition credit alone would be worth $840, so the training credit adds $1,720: each dollar of it replaces a dollar of fees that would otherwise earn 14 cents. The limit grows by CAD 250 a year because the income test is assumed to be met every year. The tuition credit is non-refundable: it is used only against federal tax, and any unused part carries forward or can be transferred. Provincial and territorial credits are not included.

The central idea

Adults aged 26 to 65 who work and file a return build up CAD 250 a year of Canada training credit limit, to a lifetime maximum of CAD 5,000. When you pay eligible fees to a Canadian institution, the credit refunds the smaller of your limit and half the fees, even if you owe no tax. The fees it covers no longer count for the 14% federal tuition credit, so each dollar of training credit is really worth 86 cents more than you would get otherwise. By 2026 nobody can have more than CAD 1,750, and most claims are far smaller: CRA counted 643,900 claims averaging about CAD 387 for 2024.

01

A refundable credit most adults never use

Paying for a course as a working adult usually brings one federal tax break: the tuition tax credit, worth 14% of eligible fees in 2026, but only against tax you owe. The Canada training credit (CTC), available since the 2020 tax year, adds a second one that is refundable: CRA pays it even if you owe no tax at all.

The CTC has its own running balance, the Canada training credit limit (CTCL), which grows by CAD 250 in each year you qualify and is printed on your notice of assessment. The questions a household faces are: how large is my limit, how much of a course will it cover, how does it interact with the tuition credit, and is it worth waiting for the limit to grow before enrolling? The calculator follows the rules for each.

02

How the limit builds up

Under section 122.91 of the Income Tax Act, your limit for a year is nil unless you are at least 26 and under 66 at the end of that year. Otherwise, it is last year’s limit, plus CAD 250 if you qualified last year, minus any CTC you claimed last year, and never more than CAD 5,000 minus all the CTC you have ever claimed. You qualify for the CAD 250 in a year when you:

  • filed a tax return and were resident in Canada all year;
  • had working income (employment and self-employment earnings, plus EI maternity or parental benefits and similar Quebec parental benefits) at or above an indexed threshold; and
  • had net income no higher than the top of the 26% federal bracket.

CRA publishes the thresholds each January. Its indexation page, dated 12 March 2026, lists them as follows. The year shown is the year whose limit receives the CAD 250; the income tested is the year before.

Limit forIncome testedMinimum working incomeMaximum net income
20252024CAD 11,821CAD 173,205
20262025CAD 12,058CAD 177,882

For the 2027 limit, 2026 net income will be compared with CAD 181,440, the top of the 2026 26% bracket on CRA’s rate page; the 2027 working income threshold is not yet published. Because the first CAD 250 was added for 2020, the most anyone can have for 2026 is CAD 1,750 (seven years), and the CAD 5,000 lifetime cap cannot bind before 2039. The CAD 250 and the CAD 5,000 are not indexed.

03

How much comes back, and what it does to the tuition credit

CRA’s Canada training credit page and Schedule 11 set the claim. On Schedule 11, line 1 is eligible fees paid to Canadian institutions for the year (more than CAD 100 per institution). The credit is the lesser of your limit and 50% of line 1, entered on line 45350. Then, on line 6, the amount you claim is subtracted from your fees before the tuition amount is worked out.

That subtraction matters. A dollar of fees covered by the CTC no longer earns the 14% tuition credit, so the CTC is worth 86 cents more per dollar than the tuition credit alone, not a full extra dollar. Up to fees of twice your limit, the two credits together return 57% of what you paid federally: 50% from the CTC and 14% of the other half. Past that point, each extra dollar of fees earns only 14%, and only if you owe federal tax, as the tuition credit guide shows.

Other conditions are the tuition credit’s. CRA’s eligible tuition fees page includes admission, lab, exam and certificate fees for post-secondary courses, or occupational-skills courses at a certified institution if you are 16 or older, and some occupational, trade or professional examination fees. It excludes fees paid or reimbursed by an employer, or by a government job training program, when that amount is not included in your income. Fees paid to foreign universities go on a separate line and do not count for the CTC.

04

Four worked cases

Each starts in 2026 with the maximum CAD 1,750 limit and no earlier claims, and assumes the income test is met every year.

  1. Two years of evening courses (the default). CAD 3,000 of fees in 2026 and again in 2027. In 2026 the credit is the lesser of CAD 1,750 and CAD 1,500: CAD 1,500. The 2027 limit is CAD 1,750 + CAD 250 − CAD 1,500 = CAD 500, so the 2027 credit is CAD 500. The tuition credit applies to the other CAD 4,000: CAD 560. Federal relief totals CAD 2,560 on CAD 6,000 of fees, against CAD 840 from the tuition credit alone. CAD 250 of limit is left for 2028.
  2. One short certificate. CAD 1,200 of fees in 2026. The CTC is CAD 600 and the tuition credit CAD 84: CAD 684, or 57%. The 2027 limit is CAD 1,400, because only what you claim is used.
  3. The same two years, started in 2030. By 2030 the limit has grown to CAD 2,750, enough to cover half of both years: CTC CAD 3,000, tuition credit CAD 420, total CAD 3,420. Waiting four years gains CAD 860, which is 86 cents on each of the extra CAD 1,000 of CTC. If fees rose 3% a year in the meantime, the 2030–2031 fees would total about CAD 6,855 and the relief about CAD 3,540.
  4. Studying in the year you turn 66. Someone aged 65 at the end of 2026 can claim CAD 1,500 for 2026, but the limit is nil for 2027, so the second year of the same course earns only the tuition credit. Unused limit is simply lost at that point.

The second chart traces the limit and claims for your inputs. The third shows the kink at fees of twice the limit. The fourth repeats the course with later start years.

05

Who claims it

CRA’s 2024 tax-year statistics (data as of 30 November 2025) count 643,900 returns with a CTC claim, totalling about CAD 249.4 million. That is roughly 2% of the 31.6 million returns filed. Earlier editions show 646,610 claims and CAD 219.8 million for 2022, and 681,680 claims and CAD 245.3 million for 2023.

Tax yearReturns claimingTotal claimedAverage a claim
2022646,610CAD 219.8 millionabout CAD 340
2023681,680CAD 245.3 millionabout CAD 360
2024643,900CAD 249.4 millionabout CAD 387

The average claim is small compared with the CAD 1,250 maximum limit for 2024, which suggests most claims are capped by half of modest fees rather than by the limit. The first chart shows claims are spread across incomes: the average is between about CAD 374 and CAD 407 in each group. These are counts of returns, not of people who were eligible, and income is total income on the return.

06

Practical choices

  • Claim the full amount when you study. Schedule 11 lets you claim less than the maximum, but holding limit back does not make it grow: a dollar of limit refunds the same dollar now or later, later claims are still capped at half of later fees, and any limit left lapses in the year you turn 66.
  • Waiting adds at most CAD 250 a year. The fourth chart shows the gain from delay stops once the limit covers half of each year’s fees. A course that raises income a year earlier, as in the retraining payback guide, is usually worth more than the extra credit.
  • Keep the income test in mind in a gap year. A year with working income under the threshold, such as a full year of study without a job, adds nothing for the next year. EI maternity and parental benefits count as working income for this test.
  • The tuition credit can still go elsewhere. The part of the fees not covered by the CTC can be carried forward or transferred, up to CAD 5,000 of the current-year amount, to a spouse, parent or grandparent; the CTC itself is the student’s own and is not transferable.
  • Using RRSP money for full-time study? The Lifelong Learning Plan guide covers that separate program; the CTC can be claimed on the same fees.

07

What the calculator leaves out

  • Provincial and territorial credits. Some provinces and territories have their own tuition amounts, and some no longer do; Quebec administers its own system. Only federal amounts are shown.
  • Ability to use the tuition credit. The 14% credit is shown at full value; it is only worth that once you owe federal tax, and otherwise it carries forward.
  • Your actual limit. Missed returns, a year as a non-resident or income outside the thresholds change the limit. The figure on your latest notice of assessment, or in CRA My Account, is the one to use; the calculator only checks that your entry is possible by 2026.
  • Special cases. Bankruptcy and death have their own rules under section 122.91. Fees are claimed for the year in which the courses are taken.
